courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
md: CFI answers "is this jump allowed?" Data-only attacks never make a disallowed jump. Defences must also protect the data that decisions depend on, and the most complete answer is still not having the memory bug.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Detecting C2: beacons, egress and fingerprints
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, monitoring agents and chat clients poll on timers too. A beacon score is a hunting lead, ranked with rarity of the destination and the type of host, not an alert on its own. Allowlist known pollers by destination and process, and review the list, because an intruder can hide behind an allowlisted name.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: An API request carries two questions: who is calling (authentication, answered by a credential in the request) and may they do this to this object (authorization, answered by the server on every request).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Retired grants (implicit and password) and client credentials
md: Modern OAuth in one line: authorization code with PKCE for anything with a user, client credentials for machine to machine, and nothing that puts tokens in URLs or passwords in clients.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
md: Misconception: "HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless." They stop script from stealing the cookie, but injected script can still send requests through the user's browser while the page is open. Storage choices limit theft; only preventing XSS stops abuse.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: "No findings" does not mean "no bugs". Semgrep's own README warns that its free Community Edition analyses taint only within a single function or file, so it misses many true positives in security work. A flow that hops across files, or a source the rules do not know about, is invisible.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Vulnerability management end to end: inventory, scans, deduplication
md: Group findings by the action that fixes them and by the owner who must act. Developers do not want 300 tickets for one library upgrade; they want one ticket listing the 300 places it fixes.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
md: A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
md: Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
md: The future contract: **if `poll` returns `Pending`, the future must make sure the waker from that call gets woken later** when progress is possible. Forget it and the task hangs forever, with no error. The Tokio tutorial calls this a common source of bugs.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
md: Use the most specific operation that does the job. If a fetch_add, fetch_or or swap expresses your update, prefer it to a hand-written CAS loop: it never fails, and on ARM the compiler turns it into a tight instruction sequence, which (as of Mara Bos's tests) it does not do for a hand-written CAS loop.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Everything in this course is for understanding and defending. Only test systems you own or have written permission to test; unauthorised access is a crime in most countries.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Account recovery: the side door around every lock
md: The account is only as secure as the easiest way to reset it. If a lost-password flow needs only an email or a phone number, those become the real password.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
md: Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog, whose optimization manuals measure these costs on real chips, gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool
md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: MTD, RTO and RPO: the arithmetic and the dependency trap
md: RTO plus reprocessing time must fit inside the MTD. A service's achievable RTO is the longest path through its dependencies, so shared components inherit the shortest targets. State RPO per failure type: replication protects against losing a site, not against bad writes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Designing the backup set: 3-2-1-1-0, schedules and retention
md: Choose the backup type by restore chain, the frequency by RPO, the retention by how late you will notice damage (by time, never by count), and the locations by failure domain, including the provider's own control plane. 3-2-1-1-0 adds an immutable copy and zero errors on verified restores.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Exercises fail when they are rigged to pass: announced weeks ahead, run by the people who wrote the plan, on a quiet Sunday, with the expert in the room. Inject realistic constraints (a key person unavailable, the wiki down, a backup from yesterday rather than an hour ago) and record measured times, not opinions.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query the output of the patch before theirs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
md: Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
md: Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are one of the most common reasons real code needs unsafe, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
md: Do not hard-code 64 just because it is common. Query the line size: Drepper suggests asking getconf for it at build time and handing it to the compiler as a macro definition (`-DCLS=$(getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE)`), and if a binary must run everywhere, use the largest line size it may meet.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript
md: The URL fragment (everything after `#`) is never sent to the server, as MDN's URL guide notes. A DOM XSS that reads `location.hash` leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF. It has to be found in the JavaScript itself, by code review, by tests, or by browser-side tools such as DOM Invader, a tool preinstalled as an extension in Burp Suite's built-in browser that tracks sources reaching sinks.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Azure and Google Cloud: activity, resource and audit logs
md: Misconception: "the activity log shows who read the secret". It shows who changed the vault's access policy. Reading a secret is a data plane operation that appears only in Key Vault resource logs, and only if a diagnostic setting was sending them before the read.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containing without breaking production, and a cloud IR runbook
md: Contain in one coordinated window: close the source, revoke sessions and keys, cut the destination if needed, with production owners ready for the blip. Revocation without closing the source lets the attacker fetch fresh credentials; closing the source without revocation leaves stolen ones working.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Human access: LastPass 2022, Identity Center and break-glass
md: "We have MFA, so stolen passwords do not matter" is the misconception LastPass disproves. MFA protects the sign-in it guards. Long-lived access keys, keys stored in notes and anything readable from an already compromised device are outside its reach. Remove standing credentials, require phishing-resistant MFA, and treat engineer endpoints as part of production.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Least privilege, wildcards and the Capital One role
md: `"Resource": "*"` is not always a mistake (a few actions, such as `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, have no narrower resource), but `"Action": "*"` or `"service:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` in an application's role almost always is. Treat each one as a finding that needs a written reason.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: End to end: grouping a million log lines into named failure patterns
md: Cluster names come from word statistics, not from causes. Two messages from different systems that share a phrase will land together, and one rare but critical message can hide inside a big cluster. Always read a few members of every cluster, and treat the HDBSCAN noise set as a queue to review, not a bin to discard.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: Vectorized engines split work into type-specialized primitives over arrays, and pass filters along as lists of positions instead of moving data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: Misconception: "it works at -O0, so -O2 has a compiler bug." Compiler bugs exist, but UB in the program is far more common. And -O0 is no safe harbor: GCC folds `a + b < a` to `b < 0` even at -O0, and the next compiler version may exploit UB that this one ignores.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Measure time with repetitions, medians and spreads, on representative input, one change at a time. Explain each gain with counters and compiler remarks. On this program LTO gave the big win, PGO a few percent, and -O3 and -mcpu=native nothing measurable.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain squared-error regression (the L2 loss) to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: A central lookup table (key range to server) also gives minimal movement, and many databases use one. The catch is that every client must fetch and agree on the table. Consistent hashing lets each client compute the owner from the key and the server list alone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: Misconception: "root in a container is harmless because it is only container root". Without user namespaces, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp and the LSM. Remove those fences, or find a bug in them, and it is real root.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Hardened default for application pods: no token, non-root, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, explicit writable volumes, resource limits, image by digest.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Misconception: "the database is internal, so it is not exposed". Internal means reachable by every pod in the cluster unless a policy says otherwise. Treat the pod network as a hostile network.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: Legal line: everything in this course is for clusters you own or have written permission to test. Scanning the internet for open kubelets or Docker APIs, or using one you find, is unauthorised access under laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act, whatever the intent.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
md: Each test rules out one failure class, nothing more. A CoT that passes truncation and mistake tests is causally used, but it can still omit a factor (as in Turpin's hints). Lanham et al. call this a defense-in-depth approach: no single test certifies faithfulness.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Misconception: "nobody knows our format, so it is safe". That is security through obscurity. Formats leak, binaries get reverse-engineered, employees leave. If learning the algorithm breaks your system, it was never secure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
md: Do not use one key for two jobs (say, encryption and MAC, or client-to-server and server-to-client). Derive separate keys with HKDF and distinct labels.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
md: "Each server picks random nonces, so we are fine" is only true while the total across all servers stays under the cap. Ten servers each sending a billion messages a year under one key pass 2^32 in under six months. Count per key, not per server.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
md: Prefer APIs that remove choices, pin every parameter to the key, test that misuse is rejected, and keep an inventory so that when an algorithm, library or key fails, you know exactly what to rotate.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or an epilogue staged through shared memory could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
md: Reading what a server sends you is not breaking in, but laws differ by state and country, and accusations can come anyway. Collect the minimum to prove a flaw, report it privately, keep records, and wait for the fix.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: DMCA 1201 bans circumventing access controls on copyrighted works even without copying; the security research exemption (renewed every three years) covers good-faith research on devices you lawfully own, but not other laws or tool trafficking. Trade secret law cares about where your copy of a secret came from.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: ISC2: four canons, enforced through certification. ACM: avoid harm, respect privacy, report risks, access only when authorised. Menlo: respect for persons, beneficence, justice, respect for law and public interest. Ask before you experiment on people, including code reviewers.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: A learned weight is a share of a budget, not a property of the domain. Copying published weights to a run 10 times longer silently multiplies every domain's epochs by 10. Always convert weights to epochs for your own budget and data sizes before training.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
md: A match is evidence, not proof. Pattern plus checksum gives low confidence; only context (keywords, expiry dates, nearby names) raises it. Tune discovery and DLP rules to act on high confidence and review the low-confidence bucket, rather than blocking on every 16-digit number.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security II: auditing reads and the Snowflake thefts
md: Log reads of restricted data, not just changes: pgAudit object logging on sensitive columns, warehouse query history, cloud data events. Alert on sequences (list everything, stage, export, download) and on volume compared with the same account's normal.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
md: A fixed seed proves nothing about kernel determinism, and batch-invariant kernels prove nothing about the sampler. Run two separate experiments: hold the batch fixed and vary the seed to test sampling, and hold the seed fixed while varying batch size and position to test the kernels. A test that varies both at once cannot attribute a failure.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
md: Protecting the workflow file is not enough. With I-PPE the attacker never touches it: they edit what it calls. Treat everything the privileged job executes (Makefiles, scripts, test files, tool configs, lockfiles) as part of the pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: An estimate of the bound is not the log-probability. d1's one-pass mean-field estimate is biased by construction, and an ELBO estimate is both a bound and noisy. Methods that work here control that error (shared masks, many timesteps, random prompt masks as regularization); plugging a single random ELBO sample into an AR recipe is what LLaDA 1.5 calls naive DPO.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
md: Turning a seized phone off "to preserve it" can move it from AFU to BFU and lock most of its data away for good. Decide on power, isolation and extraction before you touch it, and document every interaction.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
md: Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every **offline** method (one that trains on a fixed dataset instead of sampling new answers from the policy), DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
md: Patching closes the hole. It does not un-leak what already leaked. After any file-read bug on an edge device, rotate every secret the device held and every password typed through it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
md: Evidence first, then the fix. Collect what the vendor's procedure allows before patching or rebooting, isolate without powering off once compromise is found, patch, and if compromise is possible rebuild and rotate every secret the device held or saw.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
md: Microsoft states AppLocker is "a defense-in-depth security feature and not considered a defensible Windows security feature": it does not meet Microsoft's servicing criteria, so a bypass is not treated as a vulnerability. Use it to raise the bar and to control what users run; use App Control for Business where you need a security boundary.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
md: A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
md: One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly. The coming lessons build each of these.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: Learn the map once: configuration in `/etc`, user secrets in `/home` and `/root`, shared scratch in `/tmp`, history in `/var/log`, the live view in `/proc`. Almost every later lesson points at one of these places.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Turning off password login does not help if an attacker can write to `authorized_keys`, and a private key copied from a laptop works from anywhere. Protect private keys with a passphrase, remove keys of people who leave, and review every `authorized_keys` file on your servers, including root's (`/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: Applying Level 2, or even all of Level 1, to production without testing is how hardening projects cause outages. CIS itself recommends trying the guidance in a test environment first. A benchmark is a starting point that you tailor (next lessons), not a script to run blind.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: `-w` watches are the older syntax; audit.rules(7) calls them deprecated and slower, recommending `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=... -F perm=wa` instead. Many published baselines still use `-w`, and both work. And remember the limit: audit sees system calls. Lesson 13 shows activity that never makes one.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Do not set kernel.io_uring_disabled fleet-wide without checking workloads: io_uring exists for performance, and some of your workloads may use it. This is a tailoring decision per host class (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable images make the OS read-only and replace it whole: drift and most persistence disappear, patching becomes shipping a tested image, and runtime telemetry focuses on the few writable areas. The price is new ways to debug and to run agents.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse attention (each query sees only a chosen subset of keys) or sliding-window attention (each query sees only a fixed window of recent tokens). Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
md: Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained, without a guarantee.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: Do not trust the malware's own story. A ransom note, a file name or an icon is chosen by the author. Classify by what the code actually does: NotPetya's note said ransomware, its code said wiper.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
md: Never register or contact infrastructure from a live sample without authorisation and coordination. Hutchins' registration worked out, but researchers who touch attacker infrastructure can disrupt investigations or alert attackers. In your lab, the internet is fake by design.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
md: Treat a memory image as many snapshots stitched together. A single odd pointer or timestamp may be smear; a finding that two independent methods agree on is evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer
md: Every hiding trick must leave the hidden thing working, and working things touch the kernel: they have threads, memory, handles and sockets. Look for the part the attacker could not change without breaking their own code.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: C and C++ do not check bounds or lifetimes for you. Every array index, every length and every `free` is a promise the programmer must keep by hand. Memory safety bugs are what happens when one promise is broken, and the attacker gets to choose the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
md: Uninitialized reads leak what came before; type confusion reinterprets what is there. Both are fixed the same way in spirit: never let code read bytes whose meaning it has not established, by initializing first and checking tags before use.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Treat everything inside the app as readable and changeable by its user. The app's job is to protect the user's data from *other* parties (other apps, thieves, the network). Decisions about what a user is allowed to do belong on the server.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
md: A WebView bridge turns 'which page is loaded' into 'who can call our native code'. Control both: what may load, and which origin each bridge call came from.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
